definition: Cryptic means having a hidden or puzzling meaning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cryptic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cryptic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The coach's scouting report was a single cryptic index card: 'Watch the left foot. Rain helps us.'
An understated warning is quiet but readable in one pass; cryptic goes further - the meaning is folded away and must be worked for.
Indecipherable is the far rung: a cryptic note wants to be decoded and rewards the effort, while an indecipherable one defeats every reader for good.

Puzzling says only that you are left baffled - it makes no claim about why. A strange test result can be puzzling with nobody at fault. Cryptic points at an author: the meaning was folded away on purpose by someone who could have spoken plainly and chose not to.

Coded means the meaning sits locked behind a worked-out system - a cipher, a key, a substitution table - and with the system in hand anyone can read it. Cryptic hides meaning without machinery: ordinary words arranged to conceal, so the reader needs insight and patience rather than the right table.

In the corner of every painting, the artist hid a cryptic mark - a tiny anchor crossed with a key.
Collectors have floated a dozen theories over the years; the artist, plainly satisfied, confirmed none of them.
Cryptic is right because the meaning is hidden on purpose and in miniature - an anchor crossed with a key is meant to be noticed, wondered at, and decoded.
The mark is not vague (it is crisply drawn) and not meaningless; its meaning is simply locked, and the artist kept the key.
Cryptic fits short messages whose meaning is folded away on purpose - notes, clues, prophecies.
Its neighbor enigmatic fits people and works that resist interpretation without anyone hiding a key, and esoteric fits material that is open but that only insiders can follow.
If someone meant you to puzzle over it, say cryptic.

Okafor retired after forty years as the school's custodian, leaving his successor a single laminated card taped inside the boiler-room door.
It read, in full: 'Feed it before the first frost.
Count to ten at the red valve.
Never trust Tuesday.' Nothing else.
The new custodian, Rios, called the note cryptic and meant it precisely: every word was ordinary, and the old man had plainly chosen each one to say less than he knew.
There was no key to find, no system to crack.
Understanding came slowly, season by season — the October pressure drop, the valve that needed ten seconds to settle, the Tuesday delivery that overloaded the circuits.
By spring, Rios had worked the whole card out, and begun to suspect that the old man had folded his forty years shut on purpose, as a curriculum.
